title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: On Stock Lent at Interest

When someone lends out stock at interest, they always treat it as capital. They expect it back in due course, and in the meantime they expect the borrower to pay them a fixed annual rent for the use of it. The borrower can put it to one of two uses: as capital, or as a fund set aside for immediate consumption. If the borrower uses it as capital, they spend it maintaining productive workers, who reproduce its value and add a profit. In that case the borrower can both repay the capital and pay the interest without drawing on or eating into any other source of income. But if the borrower treats it as a fund for immediate consumption, they behave like a spendthrift: they squander on idle people what was meant to support productive ones. In that case the borrower can neither repay the capital nor pay the interest without drawing on or eating into some other source of income, such as land or the rent it brings in.

Lent stock is, of course, sometimes used in both ways, but far more often in the first than the second. Anyone who borrows in order to spend will soon be ruined, and the lender will usually have reason to regret the foolishness of having lent to them. So borrowing or lending for that purpose, in every case where outright extortion is not the point, runs against the interest of both parties. It does happen now and then that people do both, but because everyone cares about their own interest, we can be confident it does not happen nearly as often as we sometimes imagine. Ask any reasonably prudent rich man which of the two kinds of people he has lent most of his stock to: those he expects to use it profitably, or those he expects to fritter it away. He will laugh at you for even asking. So even among borrowers, who are not exactly famous for thrift, the frugal and hardworking far outnumber the spendthrift and idle.

The only people who are routinely lent stock without any expectation that they will use it profitably are country gentlemen who borrow against a mortgage. And even they hardly ever borrow simply to spend. What they borrow has, you might say, usually been spent before they borrow it. They have generally run up such large bills for goods supplied on credit by shopkeepers and tradesmen that they need to take out an interest-bearing loan just to settle the debt. The borrowed capital replaces the capital of those shopkeepers and tradesmen, which the country gentlemen could not have replaced out of the rents of their estates. So it is not really borrowed in order to be spent, but in order to replace a capital that had already been spent.

Almost all interest-bearing loans are made in money, whether paper or gold and silver. But what the borrower actually wants, and what the lender is happy to supply, is not the money itself but its purchasing power, the goods it can buy. If the borrower wants it as a fund for immediate consumption, only those goods can go into that fund. If the borrower wants it as capital to employ workers, only those goods can supply the workers with the tools, materials, and provisions they need to do their work. Through the loan, the lender in effect signs over to the borrower a claim to a certain share of the country's annual produce of land and labour, for the borrower to use as they see fit.

So the amount of stock, or as people usually put it, of money, that can be lent at interest in any country is not set by the value of the money, paper or coin, that serves as the vehicle for the various loans made there. It is set by the value of that part of the annual produce which, as soon as it comes either from the ground or from the hands of productive workers, is destined not just to replace a capital, but to replace a capital that its owner would rather not bother employing personally. Since such capitals are usually lent and repaid in money, they make up what is called the monied interest. This is distinct not only from the landed interest but from the trading and manufacturing interests, because in those last two the owners employ their own capital themselves. Even within the monied interest, though, the money is only the deed of transfer, conveying from one person to another the capitals their owners would rather not employ. Those capitals can be many times larger than the amount of money that serves to convey them, because the same coins can be used in turn for many different loans, just as they can for many different purchases. Suppose A lends W £1000, and W immediately uses it to buy £1000 worth of goods from B. B has no need of the money, so he lends the very same coins to X, who immediately buys £1000 worth of goods from C. C does the same, for the same reason, lending them to Y, who again buys goods with them from D. In this way the same coins or notes can, within a few days, serve as the vehicle for three different loans and three different purchases, each one worth the full amount of those coins. What the three monied men, A, B, and C, transferred to the three borrowers, W, X, and Y, is the power to make those purchases. That power is exactly where the value and the use of the loans lie. The stock lent by the three monied men equals the value of the goods that can be bought with it, which is three times the value of the money used to buy them. Yet those loans can all be perfectly secure, because the goods bought by the various debtors are put to work so as to bring back, in due time and at a profit, an equal value in coin or notes. And just as the same coins can serve as the vehicle for loans worth three times, or by the same logic thirty times, their own value, so too they can serve in turn as the vehicle for repaying them.

A capital lent at interest can therefore be seen as a transfer, from lender to borrower, of a sizeable share of the annual produce, on condition that the borrower in return hands over to the lender each year, for as long as the loan runs, a small share called the interest, and at the end hands over a share as large as the one originally transferred, called the repayment. Money, whether coin or paper, generally serves as the deed of transfer for both the smaller and the larger share, but the money itself is something entirely different from what it transfers.

As the share of the annual produce that is destined, the moment it comes from the ground or from productive workers, to replace a capital grows larger in any country, the so-called monied interest naturally grows with it. The increase in those particular capitals whose owners want an income from them without the trouble of employing them naturally goes hand in hand with the general increase of capital. In other words, as stock increases, the amount of stock available to be lent at interest grows steadily larger.

As the amount of stock available to lend at interest grows, the interest, the price that must be paid for using that stock, necessarily falls. This happens partly for the general reason that the market price of anything usually drops as its quantity rises, and partly for reasons peculiar to this case. As capital increases in a country, the profit that can be made by employing it necessarily falls. It becomes harder and harder to find a profitable way of employing any new capital within the country. The result is competition between different capitals, with the owner of one trying to take over the line of business occupied by another. In most cases he can only hope to elbow that other out by offering better terms. He must not only sell his goods somewhat cheaper, but, in order to get them to sell, he must sometimes buy them dearer too. Meanwhile, as the funds set aside to maintain productive labour grow, the demand for that labour grows greater every day. Workers easily find jobs, while the owners of capital struggle to find workers to employ. Their competition pushes up wages and pushes down the profits of stock. And when the profit that can be made from a capital is squeezed in this way at both ends, the price that can be paid for using it, that is, the rate of interest, must necessarily fall along with it.

Mr Locke, Mr Law, and Mr Montesquieu, along with many other writers, seem to have thought that the increase in the quantity of gold and silver after the discovery of the Spanish West Indies was the real reason interest rates fell across most of Europe. Their argument runs that since the metals themselves became less valuable, the use of any given portion of them necessarily became less valuable too, and so did the price that could be paid for it. This idea looks plausible at first, but Mr Hume has exposed its flaws so thoroughly that there is perhaps little need to say more. Still, the following very short and simple argument may help to spell out more clearly the mistake that seems to have misled these gentlemen.

Before the discovery of the Spanish West Indies, ten per cent seems to have been the usual rate of interest across most of Europe. Since then it has fallen, in various countries, to six, five, four, and three per cent. Suppose that in each country the value of silver fell in exactly the same proportion as the rate of interest, so that in countries where interest dropped from ten to five per cent, the same quantity of silver now buys just half the goods it could buy before. I do not believe this assumption holds true anywhere, but it is the one most favourable to the view we are about to test. Even on this assumption, it is completely impossible that the fall in the value of silver could have had the slightest tendency to lower the rate of interest. If £100 in those countries is now worth no more than £50 was then, then £10 must now be worth no more than £5 was then. Whatever caused the value of the capital to fall must have lowered the value of the interest as well, and in exactly the same proportion. The ratio between the value of the capital and the value of the interest would have stayed the same, even if the rate had never changed at all. Changing the rate, by contrast, necessarily changes that ratio. If £100 now is worth no more than £50 was then, then £5 now can be worth no more than £2 10s. was then. So by cutting the interest rate from ten to five per cent, we are paying, for the use of a capital supposedly worth half its former value, an interest worth only a quarter of the former interest.

An increase in the quantity of silver, while the quantity of goods it circulated stayed the same, could do nothing except lower the value of the metal. The nominal price of all goods would be higher, but their real value would be exactly the same as before. They would exchange for more pieces of silver, but the amount of labour they could command, and the number of people they could support and employ, would be exactly the same. The country's capital would be the same, even if more coins were needed to move any given portion of it from one hand to another. The deeds of transfer, like the documents of a long-winded lawyer, would be more cumbersome, but the thing transferred would be exactly the same as before, and could produce only the same results. Since the funds for maintaining productive labour would be the same, the demand for it would be the same too. So its price, or wages, though nominally higher, would really be the same. They would be paid in more pieces of silver, but those pieces would buy only the same quantity of goods. The profits of stock would be the same, both nominally and really. Wages are usually reckoned by the quantity of silver paid to the worker, so when that goes up his wages look as though they have risen, even though they may be no greater than before. But the profits of stock are not reckoned by the number of silver pieces in which they are paid, but by the proportion those pieces bear to the whole capital employed. So in a given country, 5s. a week might be the usual wage of labour and ten per cent the usual profit of stock; but with the country's whole capital unchanged, the competition between the various individual capitals it is divided into would also be unchanged. They would all trade with the same advantages and disadvantages. So the usual ratio between capital and profit would stay the same, and consequently so would the usual interest on money, since what can normally be paid for the use of money is necessarily governed by what can normally be made by using it.

Any increase in the quantity of goods circulated within the country each year, while the quantity of money circulating them stayed the same, would by contrast produce many other important effects besides raising the value of the money. The country's capital, though nominally the same, would really be larger. It might still be expressed by the same quantity of money, but it would command a greater quantity of labour. The amount of productive labour it could support and employ would increase, and so would the demand for that labour. Wages would naturally rise with the demand, and yet might appear to fall. They might be paid in a smaller quantity of money, but that smaller quantity might buy a greater quantity of goods than a larger one had before. The profits of stock would fall, both really and in appearance. With the country's whole capital larger, the competition between the various capitals making it up would naturally grow along with it. The owners of those particular capitals would have to settle for a smaller share of the produce of the labour their capitals employed. The interest on money, always keeping pace with the profits of stock, could in this way be greatly reduced, even while the value of money, the quantity of goods any given sum could buy, was greatly increased.

In some countries the law has banned interest on money altogether. But since money can be made to earn something everywhere, something ought everywhere to be paid for its use. This rule, far from preventing the evil of usury, has been found by experience to make it worse. The debtor has to pay not only for the use of the money but also for the risk the creditor takes by accepting any payment for that use. In effect, the debtor has to insure the creditor against the penalties for usury.

In countries where interest is allowed, the law usually fixes the highest rate that can be charged without penalty, in order to prevent extortionate usury. That rate should always be set somewhat above the lowest market price, the price usually paid for the use of money by borrowers who can offer the most unquestionable security. If the legal rate were set below the lowest market rate, the effects would be almost the same as banning interest outright. The creditor will not lend his money for less than its use is worth, so the debtor must pay him for the risk he runs in accepting the full value of that use. If the legal rate were set exactly at the lowest market price, it would ruin, among honest people who respect their country's laws, the credit of everyone who cannot offer the very best security, forcing them to turn to extortionate lenders. In a country like Great Britain, where money is lent to the government at three per cent and to private individuals on good security at four or four and a half, the present legal rate of five per cent is perhaps as suitable as any.

It should be noted that the legal rate, though it ought to be somewhat above the lowest market rate, ought not to be much above it. If the legal rate of interest in Great Britain, say, were set as high as eight or ten per cent, most of the money available for lending would go to spendthrifts and speculators, who would be the only ones willing to pay such high interest. Sober people, who will pay for the use of money no more than a fraction of what they expect to make by using it, would not enter the competition. So a large part of the country's capital would be kept out of the hands most likely to use it profitably and advantageously, and thrown into the hands most likely to waste and destroy it. Where the legal rate is set only very slightly above the lowest market rate, on the other hand, sober people are everywhere preferred as borrowers over spendthrifts and speculators. The lender gets nearly as much interest from the former as he dares to charge the latter, and his money is much safer with the first sort of people than with the second. So a large part of the country's capital is thrown into the hands most likely to employ it advantageously.

No law can push the usual rate of interest below the lowest ordinary market rate at the time the law is made. Despite the edict of 1766, by which the French king tried to cut the rate of interest from five to four per cent, money continued to be lent in France at five per cent, the law being dodged in various ways.

It should be noted that the ordinary market price of land depends everywhere on the ordinary market rate of interest. A person with capital who wants an income from it without the trouble of employing it himself weighs whether to buy land with it or lend it out at interest. The greater security of land, along with some other advantages that almost always come with this kind of property, will generally lead him to settle for a smaller income from land than he could get by lending his money at interest. These advantages are enough to make up for a certain gap in income, but only a certain gap. If the rent of land fell short of the interest on money by more than that, nobody would buy land, which would soon bring its ordinary price down. On the other hand, if the advantages more than made up for the gap, everybody would buy land, which would soon push its ordinary price up. When interest was at ten per cent, land usually sold for ten or twelve years' purchase. As interest sank to six, five, and four per cent, the price of land rose to twenty, twenty-five, and thirty years' purchase. The market rate of interest is higher in France than in England, and the usual price of land is lower. In England it usually sells at thirty years' purchase, in France at twenty.

title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: The Different Ways of Employing Capital

Every form of capital is meant to support productive labour, and nothing else. Even so, the amount of labour that equal capitals can set in motion varies enormously depending on how each one is used. The value that this employment adds to a country's annual output of land and labour varies just as much.

There are four ways to employ capital. First, you can use it to obtain the raw produce that society needs each year for its own use and consumption. Second, you can use it to manufacture and prepare that raw produce so it is ready for immediate use. Third, you can use it to transport either the raw or the manufactured produce from places where it is plentiful to places where it is wanted. Fourth, you can use it to break particular portions of either kind into parcels small enough to suit the occasional needs of buyers. The first way describes the capital of everyone who undertakes the improvement or cultivation of land, mines, or fisheries. The second describes the capital of every master manufacturer. The third describes the capital of every wholesale merchant. The fourth describes the capital of every retailer. It is hard to imagine any use of capital that does not fall under one of these four headings.
Each of these four methods is absolutely necessary, either to the existence or growth of the other three, or to the general convenience of society.
Unless some capital were used to supply raw produce in reasonable abundance, no manufactures and no trade of any kind could exist at all.

Unless some capital were used to manufacture the part of the raw produce that needs a good deal of preparation before it is fit for use, that produce would either never be made, because there would be no demand for it, or, if it grew on its own, it would have no exchange value and would add nothing to society's wealth.

Unless some capital were used to carry the raw or manufactured produce from places where it is plentiful to places where it is wanted, no more of either would be produced than the neighbourhood itself could consume. The merchant's capital exchanges the surplus produce of one place for that of another, and in doing so it stimulates the industry and increases the enjoyments of both.

Unless some capital were used to break and divide portions of the raw or manufactured produce into parcels small enough to suit occasional buyers, everyone would have to buy a larger quantity of any good than his immediate needs required. Suppose, for example, there were no such trade as a butcher's. Then everyone would have to buy a whole ox or a whole sheep at a time. That would generally be inconvenient for the rich and far more so for the poor. If a poor workman had to buy a month's or six months' provisions at once, he would be forced to shift a large part of the stock he uses as capital, his tools or his shop's furnishings, the part that earns him an income, into the part of his stock reserved for immediate consumption, which earns him nothing. Nothing could be more convenient for such a person than to be able to buy his food day by day, or even hour by hour, as he needs it. That lets him keep almost his whole stock working as capital. It lets him produce work of greater value, and the profit he earns this way far more than makes up for the extra price that the retailer's profit adds to the goods. The prejudice some political writers hold against shopkeepers and tradesmen has no foundation. There is no need to tax them or limit their numbers; on the contrary, they can never become so numerous as to harm the public, though they may become numerous enough to harm one another. The quantity of grocery goods that can be sold in a given town, for example, is limited by the demand of that town and its surroundings. So the capital that can be used in the grocery trade there cannot exceed what is needed to buy that quantity. If this capital is split between two grocers, their competition tends to make both sell cheaper than a single grocer would. If it is split among twenty, the competition is that much fiercer, and the chance of their conspiring to raise the price is that much smaller. Their competition might perhaps ruin some of them, but that is their own affair, and it can safely be left to their judgment. It can never harm either the consumer or the producer; on the contrary, it must make retailers both sell cheaper and buy dearer than they would if one or two people monopolised the whole trade. Some of them may now and then lure a weak customer into buying what he does not need. But this harm is too trivial to deserve public attention, and limiting their numbers would not necessarily prevent it anyway. To take the most suspect example, it is not the multitude of alehouses that produces a general tendency toward drunkenness among ordinary people; rather, that tendency, which springs from other causes, inevitably keeps a multitude of alehouses in business.

The people whose capitals are employed in any of these four ways are themselves productive labourers. Their labour, when it is well directed, fixes and embodies itself in the saleable commodity it works on, and it generally adds to that commodity's price at least the value of their own maintenance and consumption. The profits of the farmer, the manufacturer, the merchant, and the retailer are all drawn from the price of the goods, which the first two produce and the last two buy and sell. Yet equal capitals employed in these four different ways will set in motion very different quantities of productive labour, and they will increase the value of society's annual output of land and labour in very different proportions.

The retailer's capital replaces the capital of the merchant from whom he buys his goods, together with its profits, and so enables that merchant to carry on his business. The retailer himself is the only productive labourer his capital directly employs. The whole value that his employment adds to society's annual output consists of his profit.

The wholesale merchant's capital replaces the capitals of the farmers and manufacturers from whom he buys the raw and manufactured produce he deals in, together with their profits, and so enables them to carry on their respective trades. This is the main way he indirectly helps to support society's productive labour and to increase the value of its annual output. His capital also employs the sailors and carriers who move his goods from place to place, and it raises the price of those goods by the value not only of his profits but of their wages too. That is all the productive labour his capital directly sets in motion and all the value it directly adds to the annual output. On both counts its effect is considerably greater than that of the retailer's capital.

Part of the master manufacturer's capital is fixed capital tied up in the tools of his trade, and it replaces, together with its profits, the capital of some other craftsman from whom he buys them. Part of his circulating capital goes to buy materials, and it replaces, with their profits, the capitals of the farmers and miners from whom he buys them. But a large part of it is always distributed, either yearly or over much shorter periods, among the various workmen he employs. It raises the value of those materials by the workmen's wages and by the masters' profits on the whole stock of wages, materials, and tools used in the business. So it directly sets in motion a much greater quantity of productive labour, and adds far more value to society's annual output of land and labour, than an equal capital in the hands of any wholesale merchant.

No equal capital sets in motion more productive labour than the farmer's. Not only his labouring servants but his labouring cattle are productive labourers. In agriculture, moreover, Nature works alongside man; and though her labour costs nothing, its produce has value just as the most expensive workman's does. The most important operations of farming seem designed not so much to increase Nature's fertility, though they do that too, as to direct it toward the plants most useful to man. A field overgrown with briars and brambles may often yield as much vegetable matter as the best-tended vineyard or cornfield. Planting and tilling often regulate Nature's active fertility more than they stir it up, and after all this labour a great part of the work is still left for her to do. The labourers and labouring cattle used in agriculture therefore do not merely reproduce a value equal to their own consumption, or to the capital that employs them together with its owner's profits, as workmen in manufactures do; they reproduce a much greater value. Beyond the farmer's capital and all its profits, they regularly reproduce the landlord's rent as well. This rent may be regarded as the produce of those powers of Nature whose use the landlord lends to the farmer. It is larger or smaller depending on the supposed extent of those powers, or in other words on the supposed natural or improved fertility of the land. It is the work of Nature that remains after subtracting or paying for everything that can be counted as the work of man. It is seldom less than a quarter, and often more than a third, of the whole produce. No equal quantity of productive labour employed in manufactures can ever bring about so great a reproduction. In manufactures Nature does nothing; man does everything; and the reproduction must always match the strength of the agents that cause it. So capital employed in agriculture not only sets in motion more productive labour than any equal capital employed in manufactures; in proportion to the productive labour it employs, it also adds far more value to the country's annual output of land and labour, and to the real wealth and revenue of its people. Of all the ways capital can be employed, this is by far the most beneficial to society.

The capitals employed in a society's agriculture and retail trade must always stay within that society. Their use is confined almost to an exact spot, the farm or the retailer's shop. And as a rule, though there are exceptions, they belong to resident members of the society.
The wholesale merchant's capital, by contrast, seems to have no fixed or necessary home anywhere. It can wander from place to place, going wherever it can buy cheap or sell dear.

The manufacturer's capital must, of course, sit wherever the manufacturing is done; but where that will be is not always fixed. It may often be a great distance both from where the materials grow and from where the finished product is consumed. Lyons lies far from both the places that supply the materials of its manufactures and the places that consume them. Fashionable people in Sicily dress in silks made in other countries from materials Sicily itself produces. Part of Spain's wool is manufactured in Great Britain, and some of that cloth is later shipped back to Spain.

Whether the merchant whose capital exports a society's surplus produce is a native or a foreigner matters very little. If he is a foreigner, the number of the society's productive labourers is smaller by just one man than it would be if he were a native, and the value of its annual output is smaller by that one man's profits. The sailors or carriers he employs may belong, just as they would if he were a native, either to his country, or to theirs, or to some third country. A foreigner's capital gives value to their surplus produce just as a native's would, by exchanging it for something there is demand for at home. It replaces the capital of the person who produced that surplus just as effectively, and enables him to carry on his business just as effectively, which is the very service by which a wholesale merchant's capital chiefly helps to support productive labour and to increase the value of his society's annual output.

It matters more that the manufacturer's capital should reside within the country. It necessarily sets in motion more productive labour and adds more value to society's annual output of land and labour. Still, such capital may be very useful to a country even if it does not reside there. The capitals of the British manufacturers who work up the flax and hemp imported each year from the Baltic coasts are surely very useful to the countries that produce them. Those materials are part of those countries' surplus produce, which, unless it were exchanged each year for something they want, would have no value and would soon stop being produced. The merchants who export it replace the capitals of the people who produce it, and so encourage them to keep producing; and the British manufacturers in turn replace the capitals of those merchants.

A particular country, like a particular person, may often lack the capital to do all three things at once: improve and cultivate all its land, manufacture and prepare its whole raw produce for immediate use, and carry the surplus, raw or manufactured, to those distant markets where it can be exchanged for something wanted at home. The people of many parts of Great Britain do not have enough capital to improve and cultivate all their land. Much of the wool of the southern counties of Scotland is manufactured in Yorkshire, after a long overland haul on very bad roads, for lack of capital to manufacture it at home. There are many small manufacturing towns in Great Britain whose inhabitants lack the capital to carry the produce of their own industry to the distant markets where there is demand for it. If there are any merchants among them, they are really only the agents of wealthier merchants who live in some of the great commercial cities.

When a country's capital is not enough for all three of these purposes, the larger the share of it that goes into agriculture, the greater the quantity of productive labour it sets in motion within the country, and the greater the value its employment adds to society's annual output of land and labour. After agriculture, capital employed in manufactures sets in motion the most productive labour and adds the most value to the annual output. Capital employed in the export trade has the least effect of the three.

A country that lacks enough capital for all three purposes has not yet reached the degree of wealth it seems naturally destined for. But to try, prematurely and with insufficient capital, to do all three at once is certainly not the quickest way for a society to acquire enough capital, any more than it would be for an individual. The combined capital of all a nation's individuals has its limits, just as a single person's does, and it can accomplish only so much. It grows the same way a single person's does: by continually accumulating and adding whatever people save out of their revenue. It is likely to grow fastest, then, when it is employed in the way that yields the greatest revenue to all the country's inhabitants, since that lets them save the most. And the revenue of all a country's inhabitants is necessarily proportional to the value of the annual output of their land and labour.

The main reason our American colonies have advanced so rapidly toward wealth and greatness is that almost all their capital has so far gone into agriculture. They have no manufactures except the household and coarser kinds that naturally accompany the progress of agriculture and that the women and children of every household make. Most of America's export and coasting trade is carried on by the capitals of merchants who live in Great Britain. Even the stores and warehouses from which goods are retailed in some provinces, especially Virginia and Maryland, belong in many cases to merchants who live in the mother country, and they form one of the few cases where a society's retail trade is run by the capital of non-resident people. If the Americans were, by combination or any other kind of force, to stop importing European manufactures and, by giving a monopoly to those of their own countrymen who could make the same goods, divert any large part of their capital into this employment, they would slow down rather than speed up the further growth in the value of their annual output, and would block rather than promote their country's progress toward real wealth and greatness. This would be even more true if they tried in the same way to monopolise their whole export trade.

Indeed, human prosperity has scarcely ever lasted long enough to let any great country accumulate capital sufficient for all three purposes, unless we credit the marvellous accounts of the wealth and cultivation of China, of ancient Egypt, and of ancient Hindustan. Even those three countries, the wealthiest by every account that ever existed, are chiefly famous for their superiority in agriculture and manufactures. They do not seem to have been distinguished for foreign trade. The ancient Egyptians had a superstitious dread of the sea; a similar superstition prevails among the Indians; and the Chinese have never excelled in foreign commerce. Most of the surplus produce of all three countries seems always to have been exported by foreigners, who gave in exchange something else for which they found a demand there, frequently gold and silver.

In this way, then, the same capital will set in motion a greater or smaller quantity of productive labour in a country, and add a greater or smaller value to its annual output of land and labour, depending on the different proportions in which it is employed in agriculture, manufactures, and wholesale trade. And the difference is very great even among the different kinds of wholesale trade in which part of it may be employed.

All wholesale trade, all buying in order to sell again wholesale, can be reduced to three kinds: the home trade, the foreign trade of consumption, and the carrying trade. The home trade buys in one part of a country and sells in another the produce of that country's industry. It covers both the inland and the coasting trade. The foreign trade of consumption buys foreign goods for home consumption. The carrying trade conducts the commerce of foreign countries, carrying the surplus produce of one to another.

Capital employed in buying in one part of the country to sell in another, dealing in the produce of that country's own industry, generally replaces, with each such operation, two separate capitals that had both been employed in that country's agriculture or manufactures, and so enables them to keep going. When it sends out a certain value of goods from the merchant's home base, it generally brings back at least an equal value of other goods. When both are the produce of domestic industry, each such operation necessarily replaces two separate capitals that had both been supporting productive labour, and so lets them go on supporting it. The capital that ships Scotch manufactures to London and brings back English corn and manufactures to Edinburgh necessarily replaces, with each such operation, two British capitals that had both been employed in the agriculture or manufactures of Great Britain.

Capital employed in buying foreign goods for home consumption, when the purchase is made with the produce of domestic industry, also replaces two separate capitals with each operation, but only one of them is employed in supporting domestic industry. The capital that ships British goods to Portugal and brings back Portuguese goods to Great Britain replaces, with each operation, only one British capital. The other is Portuguese. So even if the returns of the foreign trade of consumption came as quickly as those of the home trade, the capital employed in it would give only half as much encouragement to the country's industry and productive labour.

But the returns of the foreign trade of consumption are very rarely as quick as those of the home trade. The returns of the home trade generally come in before the year is out, and sometimes three or four times in a year. The returns of the foreign trade of consumption seldom come in before the year is out, and sometimes not for two or three years. So a capital employed in the home trade may complete twelve operations, being sent out and brought back twelve times, before a capital in the foreign trade of consumption completes one. If the two capitals are equal, then, the one will give twenty-four times more encouragement and support to the country's industry than the other.

Sometimes the foreign goods for home consumption are bought not with the produce of domestic industry but with some other foreign goods. But those other foreign goods must themselves have been bought, either directly with the produce of domestic industry or with something else that had been bought with it; for, except in cases of war and conquest, foreign goods can only ever be obtained in exchange for something produced at home, either directly or after two or more exchanges. So the effects of capital employed in this kind of roundabout foreign trade of consumption are in every way the same as those of capital in the most direct trade of the same kind, except that the final returns are likely to be even more distant, since they depend on the returns of two or three separate foreign trades. If the hemp and flax of Riga are bought with the tobacco of Virginia, which had been bought with British manufactures, the merchant must wait for the returns of two separate foreign trades before he can use the same capital to buy a like quantity of British manufactures again. If the Virginia tobacco had been bought not with British manufactures but with the sugar and rum of Jamaica, which had been bought with those manufactures, he must wait for the returns of three. If these two or three separate foreign trades happen to be run by two or three separate merchants, the second buying the goods imported by the first and the third buying those imported by the second in order to export them again, then each merchant does get the returns of his own capital more quickly; but the final returns of the whole capital employed in the trade are just as slow as ever. Whether the whole capital in such a roundabout trade belongs to one merchant or to three makes no difference to the country, though it may to the individual merchants. In both cases three times as much capital must be employed to exchange a given value of British manufactures for a given quantity of flax and hemp as would have been needed if the manufactures and the flax and hemp had been exchanged directly for one another. So the whole capital employed in such a roundabout foreign trade of consumption will generally give less encouragement and support to the country's productive labour than an equal capital in a more direct trade of the same kind.

Whatever the foreign commodity used to buy the foreign goods for home consumption, it can make no essential difference to the nature of the trade or to the encouragement it gives to the country's productive labour. If the goods are bought with the gold of Brazil, say, or the silver of Peru, that gold and silver, like the tobacco of Virginia, must have been bought with something that was either the produce of the country's industry or had itself been bought with something that was. So, as far as the country's productive labour is concerned, the foreign trade of consumption carried on by means of gold and silver has all the advantages and all the drawbacks of any other equally roundabout foreign trade of consumption, and it replaces the capital that directly supports productive labour just as fast, or just as slowly. It does seem to have one advantage over any other equally roundabout foreign trade. Because these metals are small in bulk and great in value, moving them from place to place is less expensive than moving almost any other foreign goods of equal worth. Their freight costs much less, their insurance is no greater, and no goods are less likely to be damaged in transit. So an equal quantity of foreign goods can often be bought with a smaller quantity of domestic produce by the use of gold and silver than by the use of any other foreign goods. In this way the country's demand can often be met more fully, and at a smaller cost, than in any other. Whether the continual export of these metals tends in any other way to impoverish the country that carries it on, I shall have occasion to examine at great length later.

The part of any country's capital that goes into the carrying trade is withdrawn entirely from supporting that country's own productive labour and put to supporting the productive labour of foreign countries instead. It may replace two separate capitals with each operation, but neither of them belongs to that country. The Dutch merchant's capital that carries the corn of Poland to Portugal and brings back the fruits and wines of Portugal to Poland replaces, with each such operation, two capitals, neither of which had been supporting the productive labour of Holland; one was supporting Poland's, the other Portugal's. Only the profits return regularly to Holland, and they make up the whole addition this trade necessarily makes to that country's annual output of land and labour. When a country does carry on its carrying trade with its own ships and sailors, the part of the capital that pays the freight is distributed among, and sets in motion, a certain number of that country's productive labourers. Almost every nation that has had a sizeable share of the carrying trade has in fact carried it on this way. The trade probably got its name from this, the people of such countries being the carriers for others. But it does not seem essential to the nature of the trade that this should be so. A Dutch merchant may, for example, employ his capital in handling the commerce of Poland and Portugal by carrying part of one country's surplus produce to the other, not in Dutch but in British ships. We may suppose he actually does so on some occasions. It is on this account that the carrying trade has been thought especially advantageous to a country like Great Britain, whose defence and security depend on the number of its sailors and ships. But the same capital can employ as many sailors and ships in the foreign trade of consumption, or even in the home trade when it is carried on by coasting vessels, as it could in the carrying trade. The number of sailors and ships any given capital can employ does not depend on the nature of the trade, but partly on the bulk of the goods in proportion to their value and partly on the distance between the ports they are carried between, chiefly on the former of these two. The coal trade from Newcastle to London, for instance, employs more shipping than all the carrying trade of England, though the ports are not far apart. So forcing, by extraordinary inducements, a larger share of a country's capital into the carrying trade than would naturally go there will not always increase that country's shipping.

The capital employed in a country's home trade, then, will generally encourage and support more productive labour in that country, and raise the value of its annual output more, than an equal capital employed in the foreign trade of consumption; and the capital in this latter trade has, on both counts, a still greater advantage over an equal capital in the carrying trade. The wealth of every country, and, so far as power depends on wealth, the power of every country, must always be proportional to the value of its annual output, the fund from which all taxes are ultimately paid. And the great aim of every country's political economy is to increase that country's wealth and power. It ought therefore to give no preference or special encouragement to the foreign trade of consumption over the home trade, nor to the carrying trade over either of the other two. It ought neither to force nor to entice a greater share of the country's capital into either of those channels than would naturally flow into them of its own accord.
Each of these branches of trade, however, is not only beneficial but necessary and unavoidable when the natural course of things introduces it without any constraint or force.

When the produce of any branch of industry exceeds what the country's demand requires, the surplus must be sent abroad and exchanged for something there is demand for at home. Without such exporting, part of the country's productive labour would have to stop, and the value of its annual output would fall. The land and labour of Great Britain generally produce more corn, woollens, and hardware than the home market demands. So the surplus of these must be sent abroad and exchanged for something wanted at home. Only through such exporting can this surplus gain enough value to repay the labour and expense of producing it. The seacoast and the banks of all navigable rivers are good locations for industry only because they make it easier to export this surplus and exchange it for something more in demand there.

When the foreign goods bought with the surplus produce of domestic industry exceed the demand of the home market, the surplus part of them must be sent abroad again and exchanged for something more in demand at home. About 96,000 hogsheads of tobacco are bought each year in Virginia and Maryland with part of the surplus produce of British industry. But Great Britain's demand probably requires no more than 14,000. So if the remaining 82,000 could not be sent abroad and exchanged for something more in demand at home, their importation would have to stop at once, and with it the productive labour of all those people in Great Britain now employed in preparing the goods used to buy these 82,000 hogsheads. Those goods, being part of the produce of Britain's land and labour, would have no market at home and would be cut off from the one they had abroad, so they would cease to be produced. The most roundabout foreign trade of consumption, then, may on some occasions be just as necessary for supporting the country's productive labour and the value of its annual output as the most direct.

When a country's capital stock grows so large that it cannot all be employed in supplying that country's consumption and supporting its productive labour, the surplus naturally spills over into the carrying trade and is used to perform the same services for other countries. The carrying trade is the natural effect and symptom of great national wealth, but it does not seem to be its natural cause. Statesmen inclined to give it special encouragement seem to have mistaken the effect and symptom for the cause. Holland, by far the richest country in Europe for the extent of its land and the number of its people, accordingly has the greatest share of Europe's carrying trade. England, perhaps the second richest country in Europe, is also supposed to have a considerable share in it, though much of what usually passes for England's carrying trade will often turn out to be no more than a roundabout foreign trade of consumption. That is largely true of the trades that carry the goods of the East and West Indies and of America to the various European markets. Those goods are generally bought either directly with the produce of British industry or with something else that had been bought with that produce, and the final returns of these trades are generally used or consumed in Great Britain. The trade carried on in British ships between the various Mediterranean ports, and some trade of the same kind carried on by British merchants between the various ports of India, make up, perhaps, the main branches of what is properly Great Britain's carrying trade.

The extent of the home trade, and of the capital that can be employed in it, is necessarily limited by the value of the surplus produce of all the distant places within the country that have occasion to exchange their products with one another. The extent of the foreign trade of consumption is limited by the value of the surplus produce of the whole country and of what can be bought with it. The extent of the carrying trade is limited by the value of the surplus produce of all the different countries in the world. Its possible scope, then, is in a sense infinite compared with that of the other two, and it is capable of absorbing the greatest capitals.

The thought of his own private profit is the only motive that decides the owner of any capital to put it into agriculture, manufactures, or some particular branch of wholesale or retail trade. The different quantities of productive labour it may set in motion, and the different values it may add to society's annual output of land and labour depending on how it is used, never cross his mind. So in countries where agriculture is the most profitable of all employments, and where farming and improvement are the most direct roads to a splendid fortune, individuals' capitals will naturally be put to the use most advantageous to the whole society. The profits of agriculture, however, seem to have no edge over those of other employments anywhere in Europe. To be sure, in every corner of it projectors have, in recent years, amused the public with the most magnificent accounts of the profits to be made by cultivating and improving land. Without going into the details of their calculations, a very simple observation may convince us the results must be false. We see every day the most splendid fortunes acquired in a single lifetime through trade and manufactures, often from a very small capital, sometimes from no capital at all. A single instance of such a fortune made by agriculture in the same time and from such a capital has perhaps not occurred in Europe during the present century. Yet in all the great countries of Europe much good land still lies uncultivated, and most of what is cultivated is far from improved to the degree it is capable of. Agriculture, then, is almost everywhere capable of absorbing much more capital than has ever yet been put into it. What features of European policy have given the trades carried on in towns so great an advantage over the one carried on in the country, that private people often find it more to their advantage to employ their capital in the most distant carrying trades of Asia and America than in improving and cultivating the most fertile fields in their own neighbourhood, I shall try to explain fully in the next two books.
Book III. Of the Different Progress of Opulence in Different Nations

title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Natural Progress of Wealth

The most important trade in any civilized society is the trade between the people of the town and the people of the country. Town and country swap raw produce for manufactured goods, either directly, through money, or through some kind of paper that stands in for money. The country supplies the town with food and with the raw materials for its manufacturing. In return, the town sends back a portion of its manufactured goods to the people of the country. Since a town neither produces nor can produce any substances of its own, it is fair to say that it draws all its wealth and all its food from the country. We should not conclude from this, though, that the town's gain is the country's loss. Both sides gain, and they gain from each other. Here, as everywhere else, the division of labour benefits all the different people working in the various trades into which it is split. With the produce of far less of their own labour, the people of the country buy a larger quantity of manufactured goods from the town than they could have made for themselves if they had tried. The town provides a market for the country's surplus produce, meaning whatever is left over after the farmers have been fed, and there the country people exchange that surplus for other things they want. The larger the population and income of the town, the wider the market it offers the country, and a wider market is always more advantageous to a great many people. Corn grown within a mile of the town sells there at the same price as corn brought from twenty miles away. Yet the price of the distant corn must usually cover not only the cost of growing it and hauling it to market, but also the farmer's normal profit from agriculture. So the landlords and farmers near the town, on top of their normal agricultural profit, gain in the price of what they sell the entire cost of carting in similar produce from farther off, and they also save that same carting cost in the price of what they buy. Compare the farming of land near any sizable town with the farming of land some distance away, and you will easily convince yourself how much the country benefits from trade with the town. Of all the absurd theories that have been spread about the balance of trade, no one has ever claimed that the country loses by trading with the town, or that the town loses by trading with the country that supports it.

Since food, by its very nature, comes before comfort and luxury, the work that supplies food must come before the work that supplies comfort and luxury. The cultivation and improvement of the country, which produces food, must therefore come before the growth of the town, which produces only the means of comfort and luxury. It is only the country's surplus produce, whatever is left over after the farmers have been fed, that supports the town, so the town can grow only as that surplus grows. A town may not always draw all its food from the surrounding country, or even from the territory it belongs to, but from very distant lands instead. This does not break the general rule, but it has caused considerable variation in how wealth has progressed across different ages and nations.

The order that necessity imposes in general, though not in every individual country, is in each individual country reinforced by the natural inclinations of human beings. If human institutions had never worked against those natural inclinations, towns could never have grown larger than the improvement and cultivation of their surrounding territory could support, at least not until the whole of that territory was fully cultivated and improved. When the profits are equal, or nearly so, most people would rather put their capital into improving and cultivating land than into manufacturing or foreign trade. A man who invests his capital in land keeps it more under his own eye and control, and his fortune is far less exposed to accidents than a trader's. The trader must often trust his capital not only to wind and waves, but to the even more unpredictable forces of human folly and injustice, since he has to extend large amounts of credit, in distant countries, to people whose character and circumstances he can rarely know well. The landlord's capital, by contrast, fixed in the improvement of his land, seems about as secure as anything in human affairs can be. On top of this, the beauty of the countryside, the pleasure of country life, the peace of mind it promises, and, wherever unjust laws do not interfere, the genuine independence it provides, all have a charm that attracts almost everyone to some degree. Since working the land was humanity's original calling, people seem to keep a fondness for this most basic occupation at every stage of their existence.

Of course, without the help of some skilled tradesmen, farming the land can only be carried on with great difficulty and constant interruption. Smiths, carpenters, wheelwrights and ploughwrights, masons and bricklayers, tanners, shoemakers, and tailors are all people whose services the farmer often needs. These tradesmen, in turn, occasionally need each other's help, and since they are not tied to one precise spot the way the farmer is, they naturally settle near one another and so form a small town or village. The butcher, the brewer, and the baker soon join them, along with many other tradesmen and shopkeepers who are needed or useful for meeting their occasional wants, and these people make the town larger still. The people of the town and the people of the country are servants to each other. The town is a continual fair or market that the country people come to in order to swap their raw produce for manufactured goods. It is this trade that supplies the townspeople both with the materials for their work and with the means of their support. The amount of finished work they sell to the country people necessarily sets the amount of materials and provisions they buy. Their employment and their livelihood, therefore, can grow only in proportion to the growing demand from the country for finished work, and that demand can grow only as improvement and cultivation spread. So if human institutions had never disturbed the natural course of things, the growing wealth and expansion of the towns would, in every political society, follow from and be proportioned to the improvement and cultivation of the country's territory.

In our North American colonies, where uncultivated land can still be had on easy terms, no town has ever set up manufactures for distant sale. When a tradesman in North America has built up a little more capital than he needs to run his own business supplying the surrounding country, he does not use it to start a manufacture for distant sale, but to buy and improve uncultivated land. He turns from tradesman into planter, and neither the high wages nor the easy living that the country offers tradesmen can tempt him to work for other people rather than for himself. He feels that a tradesman is the servant of his customers, who provide his livelihood, but that a planter who farms his own land, and gets the necessities of life from the labour of his own family, is truly a master, independent of everyone.

In countries where there is no uncultivated land, by contrast, or none to be had on easy terms, every tradesman who builds up more capital than he can use on the occasional local jobs tries to prepare work for sale farther afield. The smith sets up some sort of ironworks, the weaver some sort of linen or woollen manufactory. In time these different manufactures gradually become more and more subdivided, and so are improved and refined in a great variety of ways that are easy to imagine and therefore need no further explanation.

When capital looks for somewhere to be employed, manufacturing is naturally preferred to foreign trade, at equal or nearly equal profits, for the same reason that agriculture is naturally preferred to manufacturing. Just as the landlord's or farmer's capital is more secure than the manufacturer's, so the manufacturer's capital, always more within his own view and control, is more secure than the foreign merchant's. In every era of every society, of course, the surplus of both raw and manufactured produce, the part for which there is no demand at home, has to be sent abroad to be exchanged for something there is some demand for at home. But whether the capital that carries this surplus produce abroad is foreign or domestic matters very little. If a society has not built up enough capital both to cultivate all its land and to manufacture its entire raw produce in the most complete way, there is actually a real advantage in having the raw produce exported by foreign capital, so that the society's whole stock can be used for more useful purposes. The wealth of ancient Egypt, and of China and Hindustan, is proof enough that a nation can reach a very high degree of wealth even though most of its export trade is carried on by foreigners. The progress of our North American and West Indian colonies would have been far slower if no capital but their own had been used to export their surplus produce.

In the natural course of things, then, the greater part of the capital of every growing society goes first to agriculture, next to manufacturing, and last of all to foreign trade. This order is so natural that I believe every society with any territory has followed it to some degree. Some of their land must have been cultivated before any sizable towns could be established, and some kind of rough manufacturing must have been carried on in those towns before the people could think of taking up foreign trade.

But although this natural order must have held to some degree in every such society, in all the modern states of Europe it has, in many respects, been completely reversed. The foreign trade of some of their cities introduced all their finer manufactures, the kind suited for distant sale, and manufacturing and foreign trade together gave rise to the chief improvements in agriculture. The manners and customs that grew out of the nature of their original governments, and that lingered on long after those governments had changed greatly, necessarily forced them into this unnatural and backward order.

title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: How Agriculture Was Held Back in Early Europe, After the Fall of the Roman Empire

When the German and Scythian peoples overran the western provinces of the Roman empire, the chaos that followed such an enormous upheaval went on for several centuries. The barbarians plundered and brutalised the old inhabitants, and this cut off trade between the towns and the countryside. The towns emptied, the land was left untilled, and the western provinces of Europe, which had been fairly wealthy under Roman rule, sank into the deepest poverty and barbarism. While this disorder lasted, the chiefs and leading men of these nations seized, or simply grabbed, most of the land in these countries. Much of it lay uncultivated, but no part of it, cultivated or not, was without an owner. It was all monopolised, and most of it by a handful of great landowners.

This early monopolising of uncultivated land was a serious problem, but it might have been only a temporary one. The estates could soon have been split up again into small lots, either through inheritance or through sale. But the law of primogeniture stopped them from being divided by inheritance, and the introduction of entails stopped them from being broken into small lots by sale.

When land is treated merely as a means of subsistence and enjoyment, just like movable property, the natural rule of inheritance divides it, as it does movables, among all the children of the family, since a father may be assumed to care equally about the livelihood and comfort of every one of them. This natural rule of inheritance is exactly what the Romans followed: they drew no more distinction between elder and younger, or between male and female, in passing on land than we do in handing out movable goods. But once land was seen as a means not just of subsistence but of power and protection, people thought it better for it to pass undivided to a single heir. In those lawless times, every great landlord was a kind of petty prince. His tenants were his subjects. He acted as their judge, in some ways as their lawmaker in peacetime, and as their commander in war. He waged war as he saw fit, often against his neighbours and sometimes against his own king. So the security of a landed estate, and the protection its owner could give to the people living on it, depended on how large it was. To divide the estate was to wreck it, leaving every piece of it open to being crushed and absorbed by raids from its neighbours. The law of primogeniture therefore came to govern the inheritance of landed estates, not right away but over time, for the same reason it has generally governed the succession of monarchies, though not always from their very beginning. So that division does not weaken the power, and therefore the security, of the monarchy, the crown must pass whole to one of the children. Which child should receive so important a preference has to be settled by some general rule, one based not on the uncertain matter of personal merit but on some plain, obvious difference that cannot be argued about. Among the children of one family the only undeniable differences are sex and age. Males are universally preferred to females, and when everything else is equal, the elder everywhere takes precedence over the younger. This is the origin of the right of primogeniture and of what we call lineal succession.

Laws often stay in force long after the circumstances that first prompted them, and that alone made them reasonable, have disappeared. In Europe today, the owner of a single acre of land is just as secure in his possession as the owner of a hundred thousand acres. Yet the right of primogeniture is still respected, and because it is, of all institutions, the one best suited to feed the pride of family rank, it is likely to last for many more centuries. In every other respect, nothing could be more at odds with the true interest of a large family than a rule that enriches one child by leaving all the others destitute.

Entails are the natural offspring of the law of primogeniture. They were introduced to preserve a fixed line of inheritance, the very idea of which primogeniture had first suggested, and to stop any part of the original estate from being taken out of the intended line by gift, bequest, or sale, whether through the foolishness or the bad luck of any of its successive owners. The Romans knew nothing of them. Neither their substitutions nor their fideicommissa bear any resemblance to entails, although some French lawyers have chosen to dress up the modern device in the language and trappings of those ancient ones.

When great landed estates were a kind of principality, entails may not have been unreasonable. Like the so-called fundamental laws of certain monarchies, they could often keep the security of thousands from being put at risk by the whim or recklessness of one man. But in Europe today, where small estates as well as great ones draw their security from the laws of their country, nothing could be more utterly absurd. Entails rest on the most absurd of all assumptions: that each successive generation does not have an equal right to the earth and everything it holds, but that the property of the present generation should be tied down and controlled according to the wishes of people who died, perhaps, five hundred years ago. Even so, entails are still respected through most of Europe, especially in those countries where noble birth is a required qualification for holding civil or military honours. They are thought necessary to keep up the nobility's exclusive claim to the great offices and honours of their country. Having seized one unjust advantage over the rest of their fellow citizens, the nobility are then granted another, so that poverty does not make the first one look ridiculous. The common law of England is said to detest perpetuities, and they are accordingly more restricted there than in any other European monarchy, though even England is not entirely free of them. In Scotland, more than a fifth, perhaps more than a third, of all the land in the country is currently believed to be under strict entail.

In this way, great stretches of uncultivated land were not only monopolised by particular families but locked up so that they could not, as far as possible, ever be divided again. Yet it rarely happens that a great landowner is a great improver of land. In the lawless times that produced these barbarous institutions, the great proprietor was busy enough defending his own territory or extending his power and authority over his neighbours' land. He had no time to spare for cultivating and improving the soil. When law and order were established and gave him that time, he often lacked the desire, and almost always lacked the necessary skills. If the cost of running his household and supporting himself matched or outran his income, as it very often did, he had no capital left to invest in improvement. If he was thrifty, he generally found it more profitable to spend his yearly savings on buying new land than on improving the estate he already had. Improving land profitably, like any other commercial venture, demands close attention to small savings and small gains, and a man born to a great fortune, however naturally frugal, is very rarely capable of that. His situation naturally inclines him to care more about ornament, which pleases his fancy, than about profit, which he has so little need of. The fine cut of his clothes, his carriage, his house, and his furniture are things he has been taught to worry over since childhood. The cast of mind this habit produces stays with him when he turns to improving land. He may beautify four or five hundred acres near his house at ten times what the land is worth even after all his improvements, and he finds that if he were to improve his whole estate in the same way, and he has little appetite for any other, he would be bankrupt before he had finished a tenth of it. In both parts of the United Kingdom there are still some great estates that have passed without a break through the same family since the time of feudal anarchy. Compare the present state of those estates with the holdings of the small proprietors nearby, and you will need no other proof of how badly such vast property serves improvement.

If little improvement could be expected from such great proprietors, even less could be hoped for from the people who worked the land under them. In early Europe, those who occupied the land were all tenants at will. They were all, or nearly all, slaves, though their slavery was milder than the kind known among the ancient Greeks and Romans, or even in our West Indian colonies. They were regarded as belonging more directly to the land than to their master. They could therefore be sold along with the land, but not separately. They could marry, provided the master agreed, and he could not afterwards break up the marriage by selling husband and wife to different buyers. If he maimed or killed any of them, he faced some penalty, though usually a small one. They could not, however, own property. Whatever they acquired belonged to their master, who could take it from them whenever he pleased. Any cultivation and improvement carried out by such slaves was really carried out by their master. He bore the cost. The seed, the livestock, and the farming tools were all his. The benefit was his. Such slaves could gain nothing but their daily upkeep. So in this case it was really the proprietor himself who occupied his own land and cultivated it through his own bondmen. This kind of slavery still survives in Russia, Poland, Hungary, Bohemia, Moravia, and other parts of Germany. Only in the western and south-western provinces of Europe has it gradually been abolished completely.

But if great improvements are rarely to be expected from great proprietors, they are least of all to be expected when those proprietors use slaves as their workers. The experience of every age and nation, I believe, shows that work done by slaves, though it seems to cost only their upkeep, turns out in the end to be the most expensive of all. A man who can own no property has no interest except to eat as much and work as little as he can. Any work he does beyond what is needed to pay for his own upkeep can only be wrung out of him by force, never by any motive of his own. Both Pliny and Columella note how much corn-growing declined in ancient Italy, and how unprofitable it became to the master, once it fell into the hands of slaves. In Aristotle's day, things had been no better in ancient Greece. Discussing the ideal republic described in Plato's Laws, Aristotle says that to support five thousand idle men, the number of warriors thought necessary for its defence, along with their women and servants, would require a territory of limitless size and fertility, like the plains of Babylon.

Man's pride makes him love to dominate, and nothing galls him more than having to stoop to persuading his inferiors. So wherever the law allows it and the nature of the work permits it, he will generally prefer the labour of slaves to that of free men. Growing sugar and tobacco can bear the cost of slave cultivation. Growing corn, it seems, in the present age cannot. In the English colonies, whose main product is corn, by far the greater part of the work is done by free men. The Quakers of Pennsylvania recently resolved to free all their negro slaves, and the fact that they could agree to this suggests their slaves cannot have been very numerous. Had the slaves made up any large share of their property, no such resolution could ever have been passed. In our sugar colonies, by contrast, all the work is done by slaves, and in our tobacco colonies a very large part of it. The profits of a sugar plantation in any of our West Indian colonies are generally far greater than those of any other kind of cultivation known in Europe or America, and the profits of a tobacco plantation, though lower than those of sugar, are higher than those of corn, as has already been pointed out. Both crops can bear the cost of slave cultivation, but sugar can bear it even better than tobacco. Accordingly, the number of negroes is much larger, in proportion to whites, in our sugar colonies than in our tobacco colonies.

The slave cultivators of ancient times were gradually replaced by a kind of farmer known today in France as metayers. In Latin they are called Coloni Partiarii. They have been out of use in England for so long that I know of no English name for them. The proprietor supplied them with the seed, livestock, and farming tools, in short the whole capital needed to work the farm. The produce was split evenly between the proprietor and the farmer, after setting aside whatever was judged necessary to maintain the capital, which was returned to the proprietor whenever the farmer left or was turned out of the farm.

Land held by such tenants is really cultivated at the proprietor's expense, just as much as land worked by slaves. There is, however, one crucial difference between them. These tenants, being free men, can acquire property, and since they receive a fixed share of the land's produce, they have an obvious interest in making the whole produce as large as possible, so that their own share will be large too. A slave, by contrast, who can gain nothing but his upkeep, looks after his own comfort by making the land yield as little as possible beyond that upkeep. It was probably partly because of this advantage, and partly because of the encroachments that the sovereigns, always wary of the great lords, gradually encouraged their serfs to make against the lords' authority, encroachments that seem at least to have made this kind of servitude thoroughly inconvenient, that villeinage gradually died out across most of Europe. The exact time and manner in which so important a change came about is one of the most obscure points in modern history. The Church of Rome claims great credit for it, and it is certain that as early as the twelfth century, Alexander III issued a bull for the general emancipation of slaves. This, however, seems to have been more a pious exhortation than a law demanding strict obedience from the faithful. Slavery went on almost everywhere for several centuries afterwards, until it was gradually abolished by the combined working of the two interests just mentioned, that of the proprietor on one side and that of the sovereign on the other. A serf, once freed and at the same time allowed to keep possession of the land, having no capital of his own, could work it only with what the landlord advanced to him, and so must have been what the French call a metayer.

Yet it could never be in the interest even of this last kind of cultivator to put any part of the small savings he might set aside from his own share of the produce into further improving the land, because the landlord, who put in nothing, was to receive half of whatever it produced. The tithe, which is only a tenth of the produce, is found to be a very great obstacle to improvement. A charge amounting to one half, then, must have been an effective barrier to it. A metayer might have an interest in making the land yield as much as the proprietor's capital could draw out of it, but he could never have an interest in mixing any of his own capital into it. In France, where five-sixths of the whole kingdom is said to be still occupied by this kind of cultivator, the proprietors complain that their metayers seize every chance to use their master's cattle for carting rather than farming, because in carting they keep all the profit themselves, whereas in farming they share it with the landlord. This kind of tenant still exists in some parts of Scotland, where they are called steelbow tenants. The old English tenants whom Chief-Baron Gilbert and Dr Blackstone describe as having been bailiffs of the landlord rather than farmers in the proper sense were probably of the same kind.

This kind of tenantry was succeeded, though very slowly, by farmers in the proper sense, who worked the land with their own capital and paid the landlord a fixed rent. When such farmers hold a lease for a set number of years, they may sometimes find it worth their while to invest part of their capital in further improving the farm, because they may sometimes expect to recover it, with a good profit, before the lease runs out. Even so, the position of these farmers was for a long time extremely insecure, and still is in many parts of Europe. Before their term was up, they could be legally evicted from their leases by a new buyer, and in England even by the fictitious legal device of a common recovery. If they were thrown out illegally by their master's violence, the legal action by which they sought redress was very inadequate. It did not always restore them to possession of the land but gave them damages that never matched their real loss.
