Even in England, perhaps the country in Europe where the yeomanry has always been most respected, it was not until about the fourteenth year of Henry VII that the action of ejectment was devised, by which the tenant recovers not just damages but possession, and in which his claim is not necessarily settled by the unpredictable verdict of a single assize. This action has proved so effective a remedy that in modern practice, when a landlord needs to sue for possession of the land, he rarely uses the actions that properly belong to him as landlord, the writ of right or the writ of entry, but instead sues in the name of his tenant by the writ of ejectment. In England, therefore, the tenant's security is equal to the proprietor's. In England, besides, a lease for life worth forty shillings a year counts as a freehold and entitles the holder to a vote for a member of parliament; and since a large part of the yeomanry hold freeholds of this kind, the whole class becomes worthy of respect from their landlords because of the political weight it gives them. There is, I believe, nowhere in Europe except England any case of a tenant building on land for which he had no lease, trusting that his landlord's honour would not take advantage of so important an improvement. These laws and customs, so favourable to the yeomanry, have perhaps done more for the present greatness of England than all their much-praised commercial regulations put together.

The law that secures the longest leases against successors of every kind is, as far as I know, unique to Great Britain. It was introduced into Scotland as early as 1449, by a law of James II. Its benefits, however, have been much hampered by entails, since heirs of entail are generally barred from granting leases for any long term of years, often for more than a single year. A recent act of parliament has somewhat loosened these restrictions, though they are still far too tight. In Scotland, besides, since no leasehold gives a vote for a member of parliament, the yeomanry are for this reason less respected by their landlords than in England.

In other parts of Europe, once it was found convenient to protect tenants against both heirs and buyers, the length of that protection was still kept very short, in France, for example, to nine years from the start of the lease. In that country it has indeed lately been extended to twenty-seven years, still too short a period to encourage the tenant to make the most important improvements. The landowners were once the lawmakers of every part of Europe, so the laws about land were all designed to serve what they took to be the proprietor's interest. They had imagined it was in his interest that no lease granted by any of his predecessors should stop him from enjoying the full value of his land over a long span of years. Greed and injustice are always short-sighted, and they failed to foresee how much this rule would hold back improvement, and so, in the long run, hurt the landlord's own real interest.

The farmers, too, besides paying rent, were once supposed to be bound to perform a great many services for the landlord, services that were rarely either spelled out in the lease or fixed by any precise rule, but were set by the custom and usage of the manor or barony. Being almost entirely arbitrary, these services exposed the tenant to many forms of harassment. In Scotland, the abolition of all services not precisely specified in the lease has, within a few years, greatly improved the condition of the country's yeomanry.

The public services the yeomanry owed were no less arbitrary than the private ones. Building and maintaining the highways, a duty that still exists, I believe, everywhere, though with different degrees of harshness in different countries, was not the only one. Whenever the king's troops, his household, or his officers of any kind passed through any part of the country, the yeomanry were bound to supply them with horses, carriages, and provisions at a price set by the purveyor. Great Britain is, I believe, the only monarchy in Europe where the burden of purveyance has been entirely abolished. It still exists in France and Germany.

The public taxes they were subject to were as irregular and oppressive as the services. The old lords, though extremely reluctant to grant their sovereign any money themselves, readily let him tax their tenants, which they called tallaging them, and lacked the foresight to see how much this would in the end affect their own income. The taille, as it still exists in France, can serve as an example of those old tallages. It is a tax on the supposed profits of the farmer, which they reckon from the amount of capital he keeps on the farm. So it is in his interest to appear to have as little as possible, and therefore to invest as little as possible in cultivating the land and nothing at all in improving it. Should any capital happen to build up in a French farmer's hands, the taille amounts almost to a ban on its ever being put into the land. This tax, besides, is thought to dishonour anyone who pays it and to drag him down below not only the rank of a gentleman but even that of a burgher, and anyone who rents another's land becomes liable to it. No gentleman, nor even any burgher who has capital, will accept such a humiliation. So this tax not only stops the capital that accumulates on the land from being used to improve it but also drives all other capital away. The old tenths and fifteenths, so common in England in former times, seem, as far as they touched the land, to have been taxes of the same kind as the taille.

Under all these discouragements, little improvement could be expected from those who occupied the land. That class of people, even with all the freedom and security the law can give, must always improve under great handicaps. The farmer, compared with the proprietor, is like a merchant who trades with borrowed money compared with one who trades with his own. The capital of both may grow, but with only equal good management the borrower's must always grow more slowly, because so large a share of the profits is eaten up by the interest on the loan. In the same way, land worked by a farmer must, with only equal good management, be improved more slowly than land worked by the proprietor, because so large a share of the produce is eaten up by the rent, which, had the farmer been the proprietor, he might have put into further improving the land. The farmer's position, besides, is by its very nature lower than the proprietor's. Through most of Europe, the yeomanry are regarded as a lower class of people, beneath even the better sort of tradesmen and mechanics, and throughout Europe beneath the great merchants and master manufacturers. So it can seldom happen that a man with any considerable capital would leave the higher station to put himself in a lower one. Even in Europe's present condition, then, little capital is likely to move from any other occupation into improving land by way of farming. More does so, perhaps, in Great Britain than in any other country, though even there the great fortunes employed in farming in some places have generally been built up by farming, which is, of all trades, perhaps the one in which capital is usually built up most slowly. After the small proprietors, however, rich and great farmers are in every country the chief improvers of land. There are perhaps more of them in England than in any other European monarchy. In the republican governments of Holland and of Berne in Switzerland, the farmers are said to be no worse than those of England.

On top of all this, the old policy of Europe was unfavourable to the improvement and cultivation of land, whether carried on by the proprietor or by the farmer. First, there was the general ban on exporting corn without a special licence, which seems to have been an almost universal rule. Second, there were the restraints placed on the inland trade, not only in corn but in nearly every other product of the farm, through the absurd laws against engrossers, regraters, and forestallers, and through the privileges of fairs and markets. It has already been shown how the ban on exporting corn, combined with some encouragement given to importing foreign corn, held back the cultivation of ancient Italy, naturally the most fertile country in Europe and at that time the seat of the world's greatest empire. How far such restraints on the inland trade in corn, joined to the general ban on its export, must have discouraged the cultivation of countries less fertile and less favourably placed, is perhaps not very easy to imagine.

title: OF THE RISE AND PROGRESS OF CITIES AND TOWNS, AFTER THE FALL OF THE ROMAN EMPIRE.
paragraphs: The Rise and Progress of Cities and Towns after the Fall of the Roman Empire

After the fall of the Roman empire, townspeople were treated no better than country dwellers. They were, however, a very different sort of people from the original inhabitants of the ancient republics of Greece and Italy. Those earlier town-dwellers were mostly landowners. The public territory had originally been divided among them, and they found it convenient to build their houses near one another and surround them with a wall for common defence. After the fall of Rome, by contrast, landowners generally lived in fortified castles on their own estates, surrounded by their own tenants and dependants. The towns were inhabited mainly by tradesmen and craftsmen, who in those days seem to have held a servile or nearly servile status. The privileges granted by old charters to the inhabitants of some of Europe's leading towns show clearly what those people had been before such grants were made. When a community is granted, as a privilege, the right to marry off their own daughters without their lord's consent, the right to have their own children rather than their lord inherit their goods at death, and the right to dispose of their property by will, then before those grants they must have lived either wholly or very nearly in the same villeinage as the country labourers who worked the land.

They do indeed seem to have been a very poor and lowly set of people, travelling about with their goods from place to place and from fair to fair, like the hawkers and pedlars of today. In every country of Europe back then, just as in several of the Tartar governments of Asia today, taxes were levied on travellers and their goods: when they passed through certain manors, when they crossed certain bridges, when they carried their goods around a fair, and when they set up a booth or stall to sell them. In England these various taxes were called passage, pontage, lastage, and stallage. Sometimes the king, and sometimes a great lord who apparently had authority to do so on certain occasions, would grant particular traders, especially those living on their own demesnes, a general exemption from such taxes. Such traders, though otherwise of servile or nearly servile status, were on this account called free traders. In return they usually paid their protector a kind of annual poll tax. In those days protection was rarely granted without something of value in return, and this tax may perhaps be seen as compensation for whatever their patrons lost by exempting them from other taxes. At first both the poll taxes and the exemptions seem to have been entirely personal, affecting only particular individuals during their own lifetimes or for as long as their protectors chose. In the very incomplete records published from the Domesday Book about several English towns, there is frequent mention of the tax that particular burghers each paid, either to the king or to some other great lord, for this kind of protection, and sometimes only of the total sum of all those taxes. {see Brady's Historical Treatise of Cities and Boroughs, p. 3. etc.}

But however servile the townspeople's original condition may have been, it is clear that they reached liberty and independence much sooner than the country labourers. The part of the king's revenue that came from such poll taxes in any particular town was usually leased out for a fixed term of years, at a fixed rent, sometimes to the sheriff of the county and sometimes to other people. The burghers themselves often gained enough credit to be allowed to lease the revenues of this kind arising from their own town, becoming jointly and individually liable for the whole rent. {See Madox, Firma Burgi, p. 18; also History of the Exchequer, chap. 10, sect. v, p. 223, first edition.} Leasing in this way fitted the usual practice of, I believe, the sovereigns of every country in Europe, who often leased whole manors to all the tenants of those manors. The tenants became jointly and individually liable for the whole rent, but in return were allowed to collect it in their own way, pay it into the king's exchequer through their own bailiff, and so be entirely free from the insolence of the king's officers—something regarded in those days as of the greatest importance.

At first the town's lease was probably granted to the burghers, just as it had been to other lessees, for a fixed term of years only. In time, however, it seems to have become the general practice to grant it to them in fee—that is, for ever—at a fixed rent that was never afterwards to be raised. Once the payment had become permanent, the exemptions given in return for it naturally became permanent too. Those exemptions therefore stopped being personal and could no longer be regarded as belonging to individuals as individuals, but rather to the burghers of a particular borough. For this reason such a borough was called a free borough, just as the men had been called free burghers or free traders.

Along with this grant, the burghers of the town generally received the important privileges mentioned above: that they might marry off their own daughters, that their children should inherit from them, and that they might dispose of their property by will. Whether such privileges had previously been granted, along with freedom of trade, to particular burghers as individuals, I do not know. I think it not unlikely that they were, though I cannot produce any direct evidence. But however that may be, once the principal marks of villeinage and slavery had been removed from them, they now at last became genuinely free in our present sense of the word.

Nor was that all. At the same time they were generally formed into a community or corporation, with the privilege of having their own magistrates and town council, of making by-laws for their own government, of building walls for their own defence, and of placing all their inhabitants under a kind of military discipline by requiring them to watch and ward—that is, in the old sense, to guard and defend those walls against every attack and surprise, by night as well as by day. In England they were generally exempt from attendance at the hundred and county courts, and any cases arising among them, except pleas of the crown, were left to their own magistrates to decide. In other countries they were often granted much greater and more extensive jurisdictions. {See Madox, Firma Burgi. See also Pfeffel in the Remarkable events under Frederick II. and his Successors of the House of Suabia.}

It was probably necessary to grant the towns that were allowed to lease their own revenues some kind of compulsory jurisdiction to force their own citizens to pay. In those disorderly times it would have been extremely awkward to leave them to seek this kind of justice from any other court. But it must seem strange that the sovereigns of every country in Europe should have exchanged, for a fixed rent never to be increased, the very branch of their revenue that was perhaps most likely of all to grow naturally over time without any expense or attention on their part—and that they should, on top of this, have voluntarily set up a kind of independent republic in the very heart of their own dominions.

To understand this, remember that in those days the sovereign of perhaps no country in Europe could protect the weaker of his subjects, throughout the whole of his dominions, from oppression by the great lords. Those whom the law could not protect, and who were not strong enough to defend themselves, had to either seek protection from some great lord—becoming his slaves or vassals to get it—or join a league of mutual defence to protect one another. The inhabitants of cities and boroughs, taken as single individuals, had no power to defend themselves; but by forming a league of mutual defence with their neighbours they could put up no contemptible resistance. The lords despised the burghers, regarding them not only as a lower order but as a pack of freed slaves, almost a different species from themselves. The wealth of the burghers always provoked the lords' envy and indignation, and they plundered them on every occasion without mercy or remorse. The burghers naturally hated and feared the lords. The king hated and feared them too; but although he might despise the burghers, he had no reason to hate or fear them. Mutual interest therefore inclined the burghers to support the king, and the king to support them against the lords. They were the enemies of his enemies, and it was in his interest to make them as secure and independent of those enemies as he could. By giving them their own magistrates, the privilege of making by-laws for their own government, of building walls for their own defence, and of placing all their inhabitants under a kind of military discipline, he gave them every means of security and independence from the barons that lay in his power to grant. Without some regular government of this kind, without some authority to make their inhabitants act according to a settled plan or system, no voluntary league of mutual defence could have given them lasting security or enabled them to give the king any substantial support. By granting them the lease of their own town in fee, he removed from those he wanted as his friends and, so to speak, his allies, every ground for jealousy and suspicion that he might later oppress them by raising their town's rent or by leasing it to someone else.

The princes who were on the worst terms with their barons seem accordingly to have been the most generous in grants of this kind to their boroughs. King John of England, for example, appears to have been a most lavish benefactor to his towns. {See Madox.} Philip I of France lost all authority over his barons. Toward the end of his reign, his son Louis, later known as Louis the Fat, consulted (according to Father Daniel) the bishops of the royal demesnes about the best way to curb the violence of the great lords. Their advice came in two separate proposals. One was to create a new order of jurisdiction by establishing magistrates and a town council in every sizeable town of his demesnes. The other was to form a new militia by having the inhabitants of those towns, under the command of their own magistrates, march out when needed to the king's aid. It is from this period, according to French antiquaries, that we are to date the founding of the magistrates and councils of cities in France. It was during the unfortunate reigns of the princes of the house of Suabia that most of the free towns of Germany first received grants of their privileges, and that the famous Hanseatic league first became a formidable power. {See Pfeffel.}

In those times the militia of the cities seems to have been no worse than that of the country, and because it could be gathered more quickly on any sudden occasion, the cities often had the advantage in their disputes with the neighbouring lords. In countries like Italy or Switzerland, where the sovereign lost all his authority—whether because of their distance from the main seat of government, the natural strength of the country itself, or some other reason—the cities generally became independent republics and conquered all the nobility around them, forcing them to pull down their country castles and live, like other peaceable inhabitants, in the city. This is the brief history of the republic of Berne and of several other Swiss cities. Apart from Venice, whose history is somewhat different, it is the history of all the major Italian republics, of which so great a number rose and fell between the end of the twelfth and the beginning of the sixteenth century.

In countries like France and England, where the sovereign's authority, though often very weak, was never destroyed altogether, the cities had no chance of becoming fully independent. They did, however, grow so important that the sovereign could impose no tax on them beyond the fixed rent of the town without their own consent. They were therefore summoned to send deputies to the general assembly of the kingdom's estates, where, on urgent occasions, they could join the clergy and the barons in granting the king some extraordinary aid. Being generally more favourable to his power, their deputies seem at times to have been used by him in those assemblies as a counterweight to the authority of the great lords. This is the origin of the representation of boroughs in the states-general of all the great monarchies of Europe.

In this way order and good government, and with them the liberty and security of individuals, were established in the cities at a time when the country labourers were exposed to every kind of violence. But people in such a defenceless state naturally make do with bare subsistence, because acquiring more might only invite the injustice of their oppressors. By contrast, when people are sure of enjoying the fruits of their labour, they naturally work to better their condition and to acquire not just the necessities but the comforts and elegances of life. The kind of industry that aims at something more than bare subsistence was therefore established in the cities long before it was commonly practised by the country labourers. If a poor cultivator, ground down by the bondage of villeinage, happened to accumulate a little wealth, he would naturally hide it very carefully from his master, to whom it would otherwise have belonged, and seize the first chance to flee to a town. The law was at that time so favourable to townspeople, and so keen to weaken the lords' authority over the country folk, that if he could hide there from his lord's pursuit for a year he was free for ever. Whatever wealth therefore accumulated in the hands of the industrious country people naturally took refuge in the cities, the only sanctuaries where it was safe for the person who had acquired it.

It is true that the inhabitants of a city must always ultimately draw their subsistence, and all the materials and means of their industry, from the country. But those of a city near the sea-coast or the banks of a navigable river are not necessarily limited to drawing these from the neighbouring country. They have a far wider reach and can draw them from the most remote corners of the world—either in exchange for the manufactured goods of their own industry, or by acting as carriers between distant countries and exchanging the produce of one for that of another. In this way a city might grow to great wealth and splendour while not only its neighbouring country but all the countries it traded with remained poor and wretched. Each of those countries, taken on its own, could perhaps supply it with only a small part of its subsistence or its employment; but all of them taken together could supply it with both a great subsistence and a great employment. There were, however, within the narrow range of commerce in those times, some countries that were rich and industrious. Such was the Greek empire as long as it lasted, and that of the Saracens during the reigns of the Abbasids. Such too was Egypt until the Turks conquered it, part of the coast of Barbary, and all those provinces of Spain that were under the rule of the Moors.

The cities of Italy seem to have been the first in Europe to be raised by commerce to any considerable wealth. Italy lay at the centre of what was then the improved and civilized part of the world. The crusades, too, although the great waste of capital and loss of people they caused must inevitably have held back the progress of most of Europe, were extremely favourable to that of some Italian cities. The great armies that marched from every quarter to conquer the Holy Land gave extraordinary encouragement to the shipping of Venice, Genoa, and Pisa, sometimes in transporting them there and always in supplying them with provisions. They were the suppliers, so to speak, of those armies, and the most destructive madness that ever befell the European nations became a source of wealth to those republics.

The inhabitants of trading cities, by importing the refined manufactures and costly luxuries of richer countries, fed the vanity of the great landowners, who eagerly bought them with great quantities of the raw produce of their own land. The commerce of much of Europe in those times accordingly consisted chiefly in exchanging its own raw produce for the manufactured goods of more civilized nations. So the wool of England used to be exchanged for the wines of France and the fine cloths of Flanders, just as the corn of Poland is today exchanged for the wines and brandies of France and for the silks and velvets of France and Italy.

In this way foreign commerce introduced a taste for finer and more refined manufactures into countries where no such work was carried on. But once this taste became widespread enough to create a substantial demand, the merchants, to save the cost of transport, naturally tried to set up manufactures of the same kind in their own country. This is the origin of the first manufactures producing for distant sale that seem to have been established in the western provinces of Europe after the fall of the Roman empire.

It should be noted that no large country ever did or could exist without some kind of manufacturing being carried on in it; and when such a country is said to have no manufactures, this must always be understood to mean the finer and more refined ones, or those suited for distant sale. In every large country, the clothing and household furniture of by far the greater part of the people are the product of their own industry. This is even more universally true in the poor countries commonly said to have no manufactures than in the rich ones said to abound in them. In the rich ones you will generally find, in both the clothes and the household furniture of the lowest class of people, a much greater proportion of foreign goods than in the poor ones.
The manufactures suited for distant sale seem to have been introduced into different countries in two different ways.

Sometimes they were introduced in the way described above, by the forceful action, so to speak, of the capital of particular merchants and entrepreneurs who set them up in imitation of some foreign manufacture of the same kind. Such manufactures are therefore the offspring of foreign commerce, and of this kind seem to have been the old manufactures of silks, velvets, and brocades that flourished in Lucca during the thirteenth century. They were driven out of there by the tyranny of one of Machiavelli's heroes, Castruccio Castracani. In 1310 nine hundred families were expelled from Lucca, of whom thirty-one moved to Venice and offered to introduce the silk manufacture there. {See Sandi Istoria civile de Vinezia, part 2 vol. i, page 247 and 256.} Their offer was accepted, many privileges were granted to them, and they began the manufacture with three hundred workmen. Of this kind, too, seem to have been the fine-cloth manufactures that once flourished in Flanders and were brought into England early in Elizabeth's reign, and so are the present silk manufactures of Lyons and Spitalfields. Manufactures introduced in this way generally work foreign materials, being imitations of foreign manufactures. When the Venetian manufacture was first set up, the materials all came from Sicily and the Levant. The older manufacture of Lucca was likewise carried on with foreign materials. The growing of mulberry trees and the breeding of silkworms do not seem to have been common in northern Italy before the sixteenth century, and these arts were not introduced into France until the reign of Charles IX. The manufactures of Flanders were carried on chiefly with Spanish and English wool. Spanish wool was the material not of the first woollen manufacture of England, but of the first that was fit for distant sale. More than half the materials of the Lyons manufacture are foreign silk even today; when it was first established the whole, or very nearly the whole, was foreign. No part of the materials of the Spitalfields manufacture is ever likely to be produced in England. Because such manufactures are generally introduced by the scheme and project of a few individuals, their location is sometimes set in a maritime city and sometimes in an inland town, according to where the founders' interest, judgment, or whim happens to settle.

At other times, manufactures for distant sale grow up naturally and, as it were, of their own accord, by the gradual refinement of the household and coarser manufactures that must always be carried on even in the poorest and rudest countries. Such manufactures generally use the materials the country produces, and they seem often to have been first refined and improved in inland countries that were not very far, but a considerable distance, from the sea-coast, and sometimes even far from any water transport. An inland country, naturally fertile and easy to cultivate, produces a great surplus of provisions beyond what is needed to maintain the cultivators; and because of the cost of land carriage and the awkwardness of river navigation, it can often be hard to send this surplus abroad. Abundance therefore makes provisions cheap and encourages many workmen to settle nearby, since they find that their work can buy them more of the necessities and comforts of life there than elsewhere. They work up the materials of manufacture that the land produces and exchange their finished work—or, what amounts to the same thing, its price—for more materials and provisions. They give a new value to the surplus part of the raw produce by saving the cost of carrying it to the waterside or to some distant market, and they supply the cultivators with something useful or pleasant in exchange for it on easier terms than they could have got it before. The cultivators get a better price for their surplus produce and can buy more cheaply the other comforts they need. They are thus both encouraged and enabled to increase this surplus by further improving and better cultivating the land; and just as the land's fertility gave birth to the manufacture, so the progress of the manufacture reacts on the land and increases its fertility still further. The manufacturers first supply the neighbourhood, and afterwards, as their work improves and refines, more distant markets. For although neither the raw produce nor even the coarse manufacture could bear the cost of any considerable land carriage without the greatest difficulty, the refined and improved manufacture easily can. In a small bulk it often contains the price of a great quantity of raw produce. A piece of fine cloth, for example, weighing only eighty pounds, contains in it the price not only of eighty pounds' weight of wool but sometimes of several thousand pounds' weight of corn—the maintenance of the various workers and of their immediate employers. The corn, which could only with difficulty have been carried abroad in its own form, is in this way virtually exported in the form of the finished manufacture and can easily be sent to the remotest corners of the world. In this way the manufactures of Leeds, Halifax, Sheffield, Birmingham, and Wolverhampton have grown up naturally and, as it were, of their own accord. Such manufactures are the offspring of agriculture. In the modern history of Europe their growth and improvement have generally come later than those that were the offspring of foreign commerce. England was famous for the manufacture of fine cloths made from Spanish wool more than a century before any of those now flourishing in the places named above were fit for foreign sale. The growth and improvement of these latter could come about only as a result of the extension and improvement of agriculture—the last and greatest effect of foreign commerce and of the manufactures it directly introduced, which I shall now go on to explain.

title: HOW THE COMMERCE OF TOWNS CONTRIBUTED TO THE IMPROVEMENT OF THE COUNTRY.
paragraphs: How the Commerce of Towns Contributed to the Improvement of the Country
The growth and wealth of commercial and manufacturing towns helped improve and cultivate the countryside they belonged to, and they did so in three distinct ways.

First, by providing a large and reliable market for the country's raw produce, towns encouraged farmers to cultivate and improve their land. This benefit was not even limited to the regions where the towns sat; it extended, more or less, to every region the towns traded with. The towns gave all of them a market for some of their raw or manufactured produce, and so gave every one of them some encouragement to work harder and improve. Still, a town's own surrounding country always gained the most from its market, simply because it was nearby. Since the local raw produce cost less to transport, traders could pay growers a better price for it and yet sell it to consumers as cheaply as produce hauled in from farther away.

Second, city dwellers often used the wealth they had earned to buy up any land that came on the market, much of which was frequently uncultivated. Merchants commonly long to become country gentlemen, and when they do, they generally turn out to be the best improvers of all. A merchant is used to putting his money mainly into profitable ventures, whereas a mere country gentleman is used to putting his mainly into spending. The merchant regularly watches his money leave him and come back with a profit; the gentleman, once he has parted with his money, rarely expects to see it again. These different habits naturally shape their temperament and outlook in every kind of business. The merchant is usually a bold investor, the country gentleman a timid one. The merchant is not afraid to commit a large sum all at once to improving his land when he has a fair prospect of raising its value in proportion to the outlay; the gentleman, if he has any capital at all, which is not always the case, rarely dares to use it this way. If he improves at all, he usually does it not with capital but with whatever he can save out of his yearly income. Anyone who has had the chance to live in a trading town set in an undeveloped countryside must often have noticed how much more energetic merchants are in this respect than mere country gentlemen. On top of that, the habits of order, economy, and attention that trade naturally instils in a merchant make him far better suited to carrying out any improvement project profitably and successfully.

Third and finally, commerce and manufactures gradually introduced order and good government, and with them the liberty and security of individuals, among country people who had previously lived almost in a constant state of war with their neighbours and in servile dependence on their superiors. This effect, though it has been the least noticed, is by far the most important of all. Mr Hume is the only writer I know of who has taken any notice of it.

In a country with neither foreign trade nor any of the finer manufactures, a great landowner has nothing to exchange for the bulk of his land's produce beyond what feeds the cultivators, so he consumes the whole surplus in lavish hospitality at home. If that surplus is enough to support a hundred or a thousand men, he can use it in no other way than by supporting a hundred or a thousand men. He is therefore always surrounded by a crowd of retainers and dependants who, having nothing to give in return for their keep but being fed entirely by his bounty, must obey him for the same reason that soldiers must obey the prince who pays them. Before commerce and manufactures spread across Europe, the hospitality of the rich and powerful, from the sovereign down to the smallest baron, surpassed anything we can easily imagine today. Westminster Hall was the dining room of William Rufus, and it may often have been none too large for his company. It counted as a mark of splendour in Thomas Becket that he strewed the floor of his hall with fresh hay or rushes in season, so that the knights and squires who could not find seats would not ruin their fine clothes when they sat on the floor to eat. The great Earl of Warwick is said to have fed 30,000 people every day across his various manors; even if that figure is exaggerated, the real number must have been very large to allow for such an exaggeration. Hospitality of nearly the same kind was still practised not many years ago in many parts of the Scottish Highlands. It seems to be common in every nation that knows little of commerce and manufactures. Doctor Pocock reports that he saw an Arabian chief dine in the streets of a town he had come to in order to sell his cattle, inviting every passer-by, even common beggars, to sit down and share his feast.

The people who occupied the land depended on the great landowner just as completely as his retainers did. Even those who were not actual serfs were tenants-at-will, paying a rent that in no way matched what the land could provide them. A crown, half a crown, a sheep, or a lamb was, some years ago in the Scottish Highlands, a common rent for land that supported a whole family. In some places that is still true today, and money will not buy any more goods there now than elsewhere. In a country where the surplus of a large estate has to be consumed on the estate itself, the owner often finds it more convenient to have part of it consumed away from his own house, provided the people consuming it depend on him as completely as his retainers or household servants do. This spares him the awkwardness of either too large a company or too large a household. A tenant-at-will who holds enough land to feed his family for little more than a token rent depends on the landlord just as fully as any servant or retainer, and must obey him just as unreservedly. Such a landowner feeds his servants and retainers in his own house, and feeds his tenants in theirs. Both draw their subsistence from his bounty, and its continuance hangs on his pleasure.

The power of the ancient barons rested on the authority that great landowners necessarily held, in such conditions, over their tenants and retainers. They inevitably became the judges in peacetime and the leaders in war of everyone who lived on their estates. They could keep order and enforce the law within their own domains, because each of them could rally the whole force of all his people against anyone who committed an injustice. No one else had the authority to do this, the king least of all. In those old times the king was little more than the greatest landowner in his realm, to whom the other great landowners paid certain respects for the sake of common defence against common enemies. For the king to have enforced payment of a small debt within the lands of a great landowner, where all the inhabitants were armed and used to standing by one another, would have cost him, had he tried it on his own authority, almost as much effort as putting down a civil war. He was therefore forced to leave the administration of justice, over most of the country, to those capable of administering it, and for the same reason to leave command of the local militia to those whom the militia would obey.

It is a mistake to suppose that these territorial jurisdictions originated in feudal law. Not only the highest civil and criminal jurisdictions, but also the power to raise troops, to coin money, and even to make by-laws governing their own people, were all rights held outright by the great landowners several centuries before the feudal law was even named in Europe. The authority and jurisdiction of the Saxon lords in England seem to have been as great before the Norman Conquest as that of any Norman lords after it, yet feudal law is not thought to have become the common law of England until after the Conquest. That the great lords in France held the most extensive authority and jurisdictions outright, long before feudal law was introduced there, is a fact beyond doubt. That authority and those jurisdictions all flowed necessarily from the state of property and manners I have just described. Without going back to the remote origins of the French or English monarchies, we can find, in much more recent times, plenty of proof that such effects always follow from such causes. Less than thirty years ago, Mr Cameron of Lochiel, a gentleman of Lochaber in Scotland, used to exercise the highest criminal jurisdiction over his own people without any legal warrant whatsoever; he was not what was then called a lord of regality, nor even a tenant-in-chief, but a vassal of the Duke of Argyll, and not even a justice of the peace. He is said to have done so very fairly, though without any of the usual legal formalities, and it is likely that conditions in that part of the country at the time made it necessary for him to take on this authority in order to keep the peace. That gentleman, whose rent never exceeded £500 a year, led 800 of his own people into the rebellion with him in 1745.

Far from extending the authority of the great allodial lords, the introduction of feudal law can be seen as an attempt to curb it. It set up a regular chain of subordination, with a long train of services and duties running from the king down to the smallest landowner. While a landowner was a minor, his rent and the management of his lands passed to his immediate superior, and so the lands of all the great landowners passed to the king, who took charge of the ward's upkeep and education and, by his authority as guardian, was held to have the right to dispose of the ward in marriage, provided it was to someone suited to his rank. But although this arrangement necessarily tended to strengthen the king's authority and weaken that of the great landowners, it could not do either enough to establish order and good government in the country, because it could not sufficiently alter the state of property and manners from which the disorders sprang. The power of government remained, as before, too weak at the top and too strong in its lesser parts, and the excessive strength of those lesser parts was the very cause of the weakness at the top. Even after feudal subordination was established, the king was as unable as before to restrain the violence of the great lords. They still made war at their own discretion, almost constantly against one another and very often against the king, and the open countryside remained a scene of violence, plunder, and disorder.

But what all the violence of feudal institutions could never achieve, the quiet and imperceptible workings of foreign commerce and manufactures gradually brought about. These slowly gave the great landowners something they could exchange the entire surplus of their lands for and consume themselves, without sharing it with either tenants or retainers. All for ourselves, and nothing for anyone else, seems in every age of the world to have been the base motto of the masters of mankind. So as soon as they found a way to consume the whole value of their rents themselves, they had no inclination to share it with anyone. For a pair of diamond buckles, perhaps, or something equally frivolous and useless, they traded away the maintenance, or what amounts to the same thing, the price of the maintenance, of a thousand men for a year, and with it all the weight and authority that such maintenance gave them. But the buckles were to be entirely their own, with no other human being having any share; whereas under the older way of spending they would have had to share with at least a thousand people. To the men weighing which they preferred, that difference settled everything, and so, to gratify the most childish, mean, and sordid of all vanities, they gradually bartered away their entire power and authority.

In a country with no foreign trade and none of the finer manufactures, a man with £10,000 a year can hardly spend his income on anything other than maintaining, say, a thousand families, all of whom are therefore at his command. In present-day Europe, a man with £10,000 a year can spend his whole income, and generally does, without directly maintaining twenty people or being able to command more than ten footmen who are hardly worth commanding. Indirectly, though, he probably maintains as many people as before, or even more. For although the quantity of luxury goods he exchanges his entire income for is very small, the number of workers employed in producing and preparing those goods must have been very large. Their high price generally comes from the wages of that labour and the profits of all the employers along the way. By paying that price, he indirectly pays all those wages and profits, and so indirectly helps maintain all those workers and their employers. Yet he generally contributes only a very small share to each one: perhaps not a tenth to a very few, not a hundredth to many, and to some not even a thousandth or a ten-thousandth of their whole yearly upkeep. So although he helps maintain them all, they are all more or less independent of him, because they can generally be maintained without him.

When the great landowners spend their rents maintaining their own tenants and retainers, each of them entirely maintains all his own tenants and all his own retainers. But when they spend those rents on tradesmen and craftsmen instead, they may, all of them together, perhaps maintain as many people as before, or even more, given the waste that goes with lavish hospitality. Yet each landowner individually often contributes only a very small share to the upkeep of any one of this larger number. Each tradesman or craftsman draws his living from the custom not of one person but of a hundred or a thousand different customers. So although he is in some measure obliged to them all, he is not absolutely dependent on any single one.

Since the personal spending of the great landowners increased in this way, their number of retainers could not help shrinking just as gradually, until at last the retainers were dismissed altogether. The same cause gradually led the landowners to dismiss the unnecessary part of their tenants too. Farms were enlarged, and the occupiers of land, despite complaints about depopulation, were cut down to the number needed to cultivate it given the imperfect state of farming in those days. By removing the surplus mouths and by demanding the full value of the farm from the tenant, the landowner obtained a larger surplus, or what comes to the same thing, the price of a larger surplus, which the merchants and manufacturers soon gave him a way of spending on himself, just as he had spent the rest. As the cause kept working, he wanted to raise his rents above what his lands, in their actual state of improvement, could afford. His tenants would agree to this only on one condition: that they be secured in their holdings for enough years to recover, with a profit, whatever they spent on further improving the land. The landlord's expensive vanity made him willing to accept this condition, and so long leases came into being.

Even a tenant-at-will who pays the full value of the land is not wholly dependent on the landlord. The money advantages they get from each other are mutual and equal, and such a tenant will risk neither his life nor his fortune in the landlord's service. But a tenant with a long-term lease is entirely independent, and his landlord must not expect from him even the slightest service beyond what is either explicitly written into the lease or imposed on him by the common and known law of the land.

Once the tenants had become independent in this way and the retainers had been dismissed, the great landowners were no longer able to interrupt the regular working of justice or disturb the country's peace. Having sold their birthright, not like Esau for a bowl of stew in a time of hunger and need, but in the recklessness of plenty for trinkets and baubles fitter to be children's toys than the serious pursuits of grown men, they became as insignificant as any solid townsman or tradesman in a city. A regular government was established in the country just as in the town, since nobody now had enough power to disrupt its workings in either place.

It may not bear directly on the present subject, but I cannot help noting that very old families, those who have held a sizeable estate from father to son for many generations in succession, are very rare in commercial countries. By contrast, in countries with little commerce, such as Wales or the Scottish Highlands, they are very common. Arabian histories seem to be full of genealogies, and there is a history written by a Tartar Khan, translated into several European languages, that contains hardly anything else, which proves that ancient families are very common among those nations. In countries where a rich man can spend his income only by maintaining as many people as it will support, he tends to overspend, and his generosity, it seems, is rarely fierce enough to make him try to maintain more than he can afford. But where he can spend the greatest income on himself alone, he often sets no limit on his spending, because he often sets no limit on his vanity or his fondness for himself. In commercial countries, therefore, riches very rarely stay long in the same family, despite the harshest laws aimed at preventing their dispersal. Among simple nations, by contrast, they often do stay, without any laws to that effect; for among shepherd nations like the Tartars and Arabs, the perishable nature of their property makes any such laws impossible.

A revolution of the greatest importance to public happiness was thus brought about by two different groups of people, neither of whom had the slightest intention of serving the public. The great landowners were driven solely by the most childish vanity. The merchants and craftsmen, far less ridiculous, acted purely out of self-interest, pursuing their own shopkeeper's principle of turning a penny wherever a penny was to be had. Neither group had any knowledge or foresight of the great revolution that the folly of the one and the industry of the other were gradually bringing about.

It was in this way that, across most of Europe, the commerce and manufactures of cities, far from being the result of agricultural improvement, became the cause and occasion of the improvement and cultivation of the countryside.

This sequence, however, runs against the natural course of things, and so it is necessarily both slow and uncertain. Compare the slow progress of those European countries whose wealth depends largely on their commerce and manufactures with the rapid advance of our North American colonies, whose wealth rests entirely on agriculture. Across most of Europe the population is not thought to double in less than five hundred years. In several of our North American colonies it is found to double in twenty or twenty-five years. In Europe, the law of primogeniture and various forms of entail prevent the breaking up of great estates and so hinder the multiplication of small landowners. Yet a small landowner who knows every inch of his little property, regards it with all the affection that property, especially small property, naturally inspires, and on that account takes pleasure not just in cultivating it but in adorning it, is generally the most industrious, intelligent, and successful improver of all. Those same laws, besides, keep so much land off the market that there are always more capitals looking to buy than there is land to sell, so whatever is sold always fetches a monopoly price. The rent never covers the interest on the purchase money, and is burdened on top of that with repairs and other occasional charges to which interest on money is not subject. Buying land is, everywhere in Europe, a most unprofitable way to use a small capital. For the sake of greater security, a man of moderate means who retires from business will sometimes choose to put his small capital into land. A professional man, too, whose income comes from another source, often likes to secure his savings the same way. But a young man who, instead of going into trade or a profession, put a capital of two or three thousand pounds into buying and cultivating a small piece of land might indeed expect to live very happily and very independently, but he must say goodbye forever to any hope of great fortune or great distinction, which a different use of his money would have given him the same chance of winning as anyone else. Such a person, moreover, though he cannot aspire to be a great landowner, will often scorn to be a mere farmer. So the small amount of land brought to market, and the high price of what is brought, keeps a great deal of capital from being employed in cultivation and improvement that would otherwise have gone that way. In North America, by contrast, fifty or sixty pounds is often found to be enough capital to start a plantation. There, buying and improving uncultivated land is the most profitable use of the smallest as well as the greatest capital, and the most direct road to all the fortune and distinction the country can offer. Such land in North America can indeed be had almost for nothing, or at a price far below the value of its natural produce, which is impossible in Europe or in any country where all the land has long been private property. If landed estates in Europe were divided equally among all the children whenever a landowner died leaving a large family, the estate would usually be sold. So much land would come to market that it could no longer fetch a monopoly price. The free rent of the land would come no closer to covering the interest on the purchase money, and a small capital could be employed in buying land as profitably as in any other way.

England, thanks to the natural fertility of its soil, the great length of its coastline relative to the size of the whole country, and the many navigable rivers running through it that bring the convenience of water transport even to some of its most inland parts, is perhaps as well suited by nature as any large country in Europe to be a centre of foreign commerce, of manufactures for distant markets, and of all the improvements these can bring. Since the start of Elizabeth's reign, too, the English legislature has been unusually attentive to the interests of commerce and manufactures, and indeed no country in Europe, not even Holland, has laws that are on the whole more favourable to this kind of industry. Commerce and manufactures have accordingly kept advancing throughout this whole period. The cultivation and improvement of the country has no doubt been advancing too, but it seems to have followed slowly and at a distance behind the faster progress of commerce and manufactures. Most of the country had probably already been cultivated before Elizabeth's reign, yet a very large part of it still lies uncultivated, and the cultivation of the far greater part falls well short of what it might be. The law of England, however, favours agriculture not only indirectly, by protecting commerce, but through several direct encouragements as well. Except in times of scarcity, the export of grain is not only free but encouraged with a bounty. In times of moderate plenty, the import of foreign grain is loaded with duties amounting to a ban. The import of live cattle, except from Ireland, is banned at all times, and even from Ireland it was only recently allowed. So those who cultivate the land enjoy a monopoly against their own countrymen in the two greatest and most important products of the land, bread and butcher's meat. Although these encouragements are, at bottom, perhaps entirely illusory, as I shall try to show later, they at least clearly demonstrate the legislature's good intention to favour agriculture. But far more important than any of them, the yeomanry of England are made as secure, independent, and respectable as the law can make them. No country, then, where the right of primogeniture applies, where tithes are paid, and where entails, though against the spirit of the law, are admitted in some cases, can give more encouragement to agriculture than England. And yet this is the state of its cultivation. What would it have been if the law had given no direct encouragement to agriculture beyond what flows indirectly from the progress of commerce, and had left the yeomanry in the same condition as in most other European countries? It is now more than two hundred years since the beginning of Elizabeth's reign, a span as long as human prosperity usually lasts.

France seems to have enjoyed a considerable share of foreign commerce nearly a century before England became known as a commercial country. The French navy was considerable, by the standards of the time, before Charles VIII's expedition to Naples. Yet the cultivation and improvement of France is, on the whole, inferior to England's. The country's law has never given agriculture the same direct encouragement.

The foreign commerce of Spain and Portugal with the rest of Europe, though carried on chiefly in foreign ships, is very considerable. Their trade with their own colonies is carried on in their own ships and is much larger, owing to the great wealth and extent of those colonies. But it has never brought any significant manufactures for distant markets into either country, and most of both still lies uncultivated. Portugal's foreign commerce is older than that of any great country in Europe except Italy.

Italy is the only great country in Europe that seems to have been cultivated and improved in every part through foreign commerce and manufactures for distant markets. Before Charles VIII's invasion, Italy, according to Guicciardini, was cultivated no less in its most mountainous and barren parts than in its flattest and most fertile ones. The country's favourable position, and the large number of independent states then existing within it, probably contributed a good deal to this widespread cultivation. It is also possible, despite this sweeping statement by one of the most judicious and cautious of modern historians, that Italy was not at that time any better cultivated than England is now.

The capital that any country gains through commerce and manufactures is always a very precarious and uncertain possession, until some part of it has been secured and made real in the cultivation and improvement of its land. A merchant, as has rightly been said, is not necessarily the citizen of any particular country. It largely makes no difference to him from what place he carries on his trade, and a very slight annoyance will make him move his capital, and with it all the industry it supports, from one country to another. No part of that capital can be said to belong to any particular country until it has been spread, as it were, over the face of that country, either in buildings or in lasting improvements to the land. No trace now remains of the great wealth said to have been held by most of the Hanse Towns, except in the obscure histories of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. It is even uncertain where some of them stood, or which towns in Europe the Latin names given to some of them refer to. But although the misfortunes of Italy at the end of the fifteenth and the start of the sixteenth centuries greatly reduced the commerce and manufactures of the cities of Lombardy and Tuscany, those regions are still among the most populous and best cultivated in Europe. The civil wars of Flanders, and the Spanish government that followed them, drove away the great commerce of Antwerp, Ghent, and Bruges. Yet Flanders is still one of the richest, best cultivated, and most populous provinces of Europe. The ordinary upheavals of war and government easily dry up the sources of wealth that come from commerce alone. Wealth that comes from the more solid improvements of agriculture is far more durable, and can only be destroyed by those more violent convulsions caused by the depredations of hostile and barbarous nations carried on for a century or two together, like those that happened for a time before and after the fall of the Roman empire in the western provinces of Europe.
Book IV. Of Systems of Political Economy

Political economy, regarded as a branch of the science of a statesman or legislator, sets out two distinct aims: first, to provide a plentiful revenue or subsistence for the people, or more precisely, to enable them to provide such a revenue or subsistence for themselves; and second, to supply the state or commonwealth with revenue enough for public services. It aims to enrich both the people and the sovereign.

The differing pace at which wealth has grown in different ages and nations has given rise to two different systems of political economy for enriching the people. One may be called the system of commerce, the other the system of agriculture. I shall try to explain both as fully and clearly as I can, and I shall begin with the system of commerce. It is the modern system, and is best understood in our own country and our own times.
